## Results

### Data summary

After quality control filtering, 12,163 valid observation-days across
35 calendar years (1986--2025) were available for analysis. The
overall circular mean peak hour was 15:58 local time
(circular SD = 2.84 h), confirming that the daily maximum at
Épinal typically occurs in the mid-afternoon, consistent with
boundary-layer heating dynamics (Supplementary Figure~\ref{fig-context}).

### Year--season interaction test

I first tested whether the year-slope differs across meteorological
seasons using a likelihood-ratio (LR) test comparing nested von Mises
GLMs (Methods). The interaction was significant ($\chi^2 = 13.71$,
df = 3, $p = 0.0033$), rejecting the null hypothesis that all four
seasons share a common trend. This result justifies examining seasonal
estimates as the primary analytical framework rather than a single
pooled estimate.

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

### Spring (March--May)

The von Mises regression for spring yields a slope of $-0.065$ h/decade
(95\% bootstrap CI: $-0.145$, $+0.027$; Wald $p = 0.17$), corresponding
to approximately $-3.9$ min/decade. This estimate does not survive
Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction at $\alpha = 0.05$.

Sensitivity analysis confirms the near-zero nature of the spring
estimate across methodological choices:

| Variant | $\beta$ (h/decade) |
|---------|-------------------:|
| Primary (earliest tie) | $-0.065$ |
| Latest tie | $-0.070$ |
| 3-hour subsampling | $-0.059$ |
| 6-hour subsampling | $-0.079$ |
| Min amplitude 1.0$\,^\circ$C | $-0.065$ |
| Min amplitude 3.0$\,^\circ$C | $-0.070$ |

All spring sensitivity variants remain within $\pm 0.015$ h/decade of
the primary estimate, indicating no evidence of a trend regardless of
methodological choice.

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

### Summer (June--August)

Summer shows a near-zero slope of $+0.020$ h/decade (95\% bootstrap CI:
$-0.081$, $+0.118$; Wald $p = 0.68$), corresponding to approximately
$+1.2$ min/decade. This is not significant after FDR correction.

Sensitivity estimates are similarly centred near zero:

| Variant | $\beta$ (h/decade) |
|---------|-------------------:|
| Primary (earliest tie) | $+0.020$ |
| Latest tie | $+0.037$ |
| 3-hour subsampling | $+0.028$ |
| 6-hour subsampling | $-0.017$ |
| Min amplitude 1.0$\,^\circ$C | $+0.020$ |
| Min amplitude 3.0$\,^\circ$C | $+0.023$ |

The 6-hour subsampling variant flips sign, confirming that the summer
estimate is indistinguishable from zero and sensitive to discretisation
choice.

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

### Autumn (September--November)

Autumn exhibits a moderate delay of $+0.085$ h/decade (95\% bootstrap
CI: $-0.018$, $+0.189$; Wald $p = 0.10$), corresponding to
approximately $+5.1$ min/decade. While the point estimate is the second
largest in magnitude after winter, it does not survive FDR correction.

The positive direction is consistent across all sensitivity variants:

| Variant | $\beta$ (h/decade) |
|---------|-------------------:|
| Primary (earliest tie) | $+0.085$ |
| Latest tie | $+0.063$ |
| 3-hour subsampling | $+0.101$ |
| 6-hour subsampling | $+0.098$ |
| Min amplitude 1.0$\,^\circ$C | $+0.085$ |
| Min amplitude 3.0$\,^\circ$C | $+0.085$ |

All six variants produce positive estimates ranging from $+0.06$ to
$+0.10$ h/decade. While non-significant, the directional consistency
across variants suggests this may be a real but weak signal that the
current record lacks power to detect.

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

### Winter (December--February)

Winter shows the largest and only statistically significant shift: an
advance of $-0.189$ h/decade (95\% bootstrap CI: $-0.342$, $-0.026$;
Wald $p = 0.0015$), corresponding to approximately $-11.3$ min/decade.
This estimate survives Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction at
$\alpha = 0.05$.

The advance is directionally robust across all sensitivity variants:

| Variant | $\beta$ (h/decade) |
|---------|-------------------:|
| Primary (earliest tie) | $-0.189$ |
| Latest tie | $-0.215$ |
| 3-hour subsampling | $-0.198$ |
| 6-hour subsampling | $-0.302$ |
| Min amplitude 1.0$\,^\circ$C | $-0.189$ |
| Min amplitude 3.0$\,^\circ$C | $-0.130$ |

Every sensitivity variant yields a negative estimate (range:
$-0.13$ to $-0.30$ h/decade), confirming the winter advance is not an
artefact of parameter choice. The amplitude and magnitude are
consistently greater than the other three seasons.

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

### Seasonal summary

All four seasonal estimates are summarised in
Table~\ref{tbl-seasonal-primary}. Only winter is significant after FDR
correction.

| Season | $\beta$ (h/decade) | 95\% bootstrap CI | Wald $p$ | BH rejected |
|--------|--------------------:|:-----------------:|:--------:|:-----------:|
| Spring (MAM) | $-0.065$ | $(-0.145, +0.027)$ | 0.17 | No |
| Summer (JJA) | $+0.020$ | $(-0.081, +0.118)$ | 0.68 | No |
| Autumn (SON) | $+0.085$ | $(-0.018, +0.189)$ | 0.10 | No |
| Winter (DJF) | $-0.189$ | $(-0.342, -0.026)$ | 0.0015 | Yes |

: Per-season slope estimates from the year--season interaction von
Mises GLM. Wald $p$-values are corrected via the Benjamini-Hochberg
procedure ($\alpha = 0.05$, $m = 4$). Bootstrap CIs are 2.5th and 97.5th
percentiles from 1,000 resamples. {#tbl-seasonal-primary}

### Supplementary: pooled (all-season) estimate

For comparison with previous studies that report only annual-scale
estimates, I also fit the von Mises GLM to all observations pooled
across seasons. The pooled slope is $-0.028$ h/decade (95\% bootstrap
CI: $-0.070$, $+0.012$), corresponding to approximately $-1.7$ min/decade
(95\% CI: $-4.2$ to $+0.7$ min/decade).

This near-zero pooled estimate masks the opposing winter (negative) and
autumn (positive) trends, which cancel when aggregated --- a classic
Simpson's paradox. The pooled result should therefore be interpreted as
the annual average of heterogeneous seasonal signals rather than as a
primary finding.

Six methodological variants applied to the pooled data all remain
consistent with the null (full results in Supplementary S2).

Figure~\ref{fig-wrapped-scatter} shows the daily peak-hour observations
with the fitted pooled trend line and 95% confidence band.

### Supplementary analyses

Temperature-weighted von Mises regression (weighting each day by its
diurnal amplitude) produced an estimate of $+0.021$ h/decade
(95\% CI: $-0.013$ to $+0.053$), consistent with the pooled result.
The circular--linear rank correlation (Mardia 1976) yielded
$\rho_c = 0.025$ ($p = 0.021$), suggesting a very weak but statistically
detectable association.
